questions.stem: The Earth's early atmosphere was mainly carbon dioxide with little oxygen. Today it is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen. What process was primarily responsible for this dramatic change?

options.text: Volcanic eruptions released oxygen into the atmosphere
Photosynthesis by early plants and algae converted CO₂ into O₂ over billions of years
The Sun's radiation split CO₂ molecules into carbon and oxygen
Animals breathing out oxygen increased its concentration

questions.explanation: Photosynthetic organisms (first cyanobacteria, then algae and plants) absorbed carbon dioxide and released oxygen: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Over billions of years, this gradually increased oxygen levels and decreased CO₂ levels. Animals breathe in oxygen and breathe out CO₂, so they consume rather than produce oxygen.

questions.stem: A student says the atmosphere is about 21% oxygen and 78% nitrogen, with the remaining 1% being entirely carbon dioxide. Why is this inaccurate?

options.text: The 1% is entirely water vapour
The remaining 1% is mainly argon (about 0.93%), with small amounts of CO₂ (about 0.04%) and traces of other gases
There is actually 5% carbon dioxide in the atmosphere
The atmosphere contains no carbon dioxide at all

questions.explanation: The approximately 1% that is not nitrogen or oxygen is mostly argon (0.93%), a noble gas. Carbon dioxide makes up only about 0.04% (400 ppm) of the atmosphere — a very small proportion, though even this small amount has a significant effect on climate. Water vapour is variable and also present in small amounts.

questions.stem: The early atmosphere's high CO₂ levels decreased over time through two main processes: photosynthesis and another geological process. What was this second process?

options.text: CO₂ was destroyed by lightning
CO₂ dissolved in the oceans and was locked up in sedimentary rocks (limestone) and fossil fuels
CO₂ escaped into space
CO₂ was converted to nitrogen by bacteria

questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans, where marine organisms used it to make calcium carbonate shells. When these organisms died, their shells formed sedimentary rocks like limestone (CaCO₃). Carbon was also locked up in fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) formed from the remains of organisms. These processes removed vast amounts of CO₂ from the atmosphere over geological time.

questions.stem: Scientists study air bubbles trapped in ancient ice cores to determine the composition of past atmospheres. An ice core from 800,000 years ago shows CO₂ levels of about 180 ppm. Current levels are about 420 ppm. What does this data suggest?

options.text: CO₂ levels have always been constant throughout history
CO₂ levels have more than doubled, with the recent rapid increase coinciding with industrialisation and fossil fuel burning
CO₂ levels were higher in the past than they are now
Ice cores cannot provide reliable information about past atmospheres

questions.explanation: Ice cores provide direct evidence of past atmospheric composition. The data shows that CO₂ levels fluctuated naturally between about 180-280 ppm over 800,000 years, but have risen sharply to over 420 ppm since the Industrial Revolution (mid-1800s). This rapid increase correlates with the burning of fossil fuels, which releases CO₂ stored millions of years ago.

questions.stem: Nitrogen makes up 78% of the atmosphere but is relatively unreactive. Why is nitrogen so stable, and what eventually makes it available to plants?

options.text: Nitrogen atoms have full outer shells and never react
N₂ has a very strong triple bond (N≡N) that is hard to break; nitrogen-fixing bacteria and lightning can break it to form compounds plants can use
Plants absorb nitrogen gas directly through their leaves
Nitrogen is only used by animals, not plants

questions.explanation: The N₂ molecule has a very strong triple covalent bond (N≡N) requiring a lot of energy to break, making nitrogen gas very unreactive. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in soil and root nodules of legumes can break this bond, converting N₂ into ammonia (NH₃) and nitrates that plants can absorb. Lightning also provides enough energy to break the triple bond, forming nitrogen oxides.
